title: The Law Points Out Sin
english: […] set it up at the crossroads, and so made plain to those on the road what lay in their path, not so that they would stumble over these things again, but rather so that they might step over them and escape the harm. Did the light, then, do them wrong because it showed them what was hurting them? Or shall we say instead that it did them the greatest possible good and made them safer? This, I think, is clear to everyone.

So when we, who were sinners and stumbled into a great many offenses, came to know sin through the law, the law could not reasonably be thought or called sin, far from it. Rather, as I said, it is what points sin out.

“For I would not have known covetous desire if the law had not said, ‘You shall not covet.’ But sin, seizing an occasion through the commandment, produced in me every kind of covetous desire” (Romans 7:7–8; Exodus 20:17). Here he also brings in the weakness of our nature: the law, given for our benefit, turned against us when no one expected it, as the light of the sun does to those whose eyes are weak. So when he says that the commandment in a way became an occasion for desires, let no one suppose that he is accusing the law. He is rather crying out against the weakness in us, since we, who ought to have been held back by the law, are spurred on by these very things toward what is worse.

For the human mind is always sick with a love of empty things that draws it toward desires. The one who carries out his desires lives as he pleases and is left untroubled; but the one who checks them meets a fiercer onslaught of the passions. No one desires what lies ready to hand; what a person is forbidden, that he desires. So when the law forbade what does harm, it became for the weaker an occasion to desire that very thing all the more.

“For apart from the law sin is dead” (Romans 7:8). If no law were laid down, he says, to condemn the way of wickedness, evil would become powerless. For through the law it is all but provoked into strength. In some people the sting of pleasure will press with less force when no one rebukes it; it is all but blunted, charmed by the wide freedom it is given. For where there is nothing at all to resist, there the urge to contend surely lies idle as well. Sin, then, is dead when the law does not declare what must be done.

The guide into the mysteries says that he once lived without the law, and then, when the commandment came, he insists that sin came back to life, while he himself died (Romans 7:9–10). In these words he frames the argument in his own person, but I think he wishes to show something like this. It is agreed that even sinning in ignorance is liable to judgment. But that the punishment will be heavier for those who know, the Savior has made fully certain when he says, “The one who knows his master’s will and does not do it will be beaten with many blows; but the one who does not know and does not do it will be beaten with few” (Luke 12:47–48). It is agreed, then, that it is better to sin in ignorance than with knowledge of the laws. But suppose someone has come under the law after once living his life outside the law, and then, having chosen to disregard its decrees, has been convicted on a charge of sin and has fallen […]

title: Sin Comes Back to Life
english: […] under sentence. Then indeed, grieving over his own carelessness and all but crying out against the strictness of the law, he will say, “I once lived apart from the law; but when the commandment came, sin came back to life, and I died” (Romans 7:9–10).

For if sin is truly dead apart from the law, is it not reasonable to think that sin is in a way brought to life through the law? For the law makes it manifest and, as it were, puts breath into it, though it was not known before, even if it was in us. For we were not righteous; but since sin was, as it were, dead, perhaps because there was no law to condemn it, we lived, and our ignorance gave us a ready plea for excuse. “For where there is no law, there is no transgression either,” as he himself says (Romans 4:15). So when the commandment came forward into the open, sin, as it were, came back to life, and death and curse and penalty were made ready for those who fall into transgressions out of weakness.

And what came of this? Something beyond all hope and expectation happened in our case. For the commandment, he says, which was given for life, was found to lead to death (Romans 7:10). Just as the light of the sun’s ray somehow harms those whose sight is sick, though by nature it is sweet and greatly longed for, and it is not the light itself at all that does the wrong, but the harm they receive from it should rather be laid to the charge of the sufferers’ sickness, so in the same way, I think, he says that the commandment gave sin an occasion, and that he was deceived through it and brought down even to death (Romans 7:11).

One might also put it another way: the love of pleasure is always very prone, in one way or another, to fight against the purposes of the law. The ways of wickedness, when they are checked by decency, march out against it the more stoutly. At times they plunder the mind, overturning it into transgression and bringing it under the penalties of the law, though it was the law that gave them the occasion for this war. This is why Paul, wise as he is, says that he was deceived through the commandment and died through it (Romans 7:11). For in effect it killed, by sharpening the pleasures within us to resist, in the ways already described.

“So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good” (Romans 7:12). The law is holy, and the commandment holy and just and good, for it makes holy and just and good those who choose to keep it, so that they may in no way be caught by the charges that arise from transgressions. But this was, in some way, beyond reach; for “who will understand his offenses?” as it is written (Psalm 19:12).

“Did that which is good, then, become death to me?” (Romans 7:13). The law is holy, and the commandment too is holy and good. How, then, did he say, “And the commandment meant for life was found, for me, to lead to death” (Romans 7:10)? Tell me, then: has the good become the bringer of ruin? “By no means,” he says (Romans 7:13). “In these words I am least of all blaming the law; I stand, as it were, as the accuser of sin. For sin so overpowers human nature and has so mastered the mind within us that the very law given to us for salvation […]

title: Sin Beyond Measure and the Spiritual Law
english: […] and life, the commandment that is truly holy and good, became an occasion of death for those under its yoke.” How, and in what way? If penalty always follows those who break the law, and we have now sunk so far into weakness that we are always being caught in transgressions, it is already fairly plain that in this way the law that saves, holy and good as it is, seems somehow to have become the sinews of sin and a road to death for those who are under sin.

And perhaps, he says, it was “so that sin might become sinful beyond measure through the commandment” (Romans 7:13). Those who did not know what the Master wills will certainly be caught by penalties, for they have acted lawlessly, even if they did not know it. Yet they have, I think, a plea in their defense that is not unconvincing, for they will likely put forward their ignorance. But for those under the law, to say that they did not know the Master’s will is surely empty. So if such a person is seen to have chosen to live an unholy life, the charge against him will be not ignorance but reckless folly, and, beyond that, the utmost lack of love for God. In this way sin might be called sinful beyond measure. For the one who has done wrong as in ignorance is also a sinner, but he is by no means called, nor is he, a sinner beyond measure.

“For we know that the law is spiritual” (Romans 7:14). He calls the law spiritual because it makes spiritual those who follow it. And a person is understood to be spiritual who does not live according to the flesh, but has turned rather toward the wish to follow the will of the Spirit. The blessed David also said, “The law of the Lord is blameless, turning souls back; the testimony of the Lord is faithful, making infants wise. The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring forever and ever” (Psalm 19:7, 9). Just as he says that the law is blameless, because it knows how to make people blameless, and the testimony faithful, because it makes them faithful, and the fear pure, because it makes pure, so you will take it here too that the law is called spiritual because it makes spiritual those who follow it. For even if it is in shadows, it still holds the form of the truth (Romans 2:20).

What, then, does Paul do? He insists that the law is spiritual, but he blames human nature as gravely sick with sin. And he tries to convince us that, because the law is spiritual, for that very reason it is most burdensome to human nature. For what, tell me, he says, if “the law is spiritual, but I am of the flesh” (Romans 7:14), that is, ruled as by a tyrant by the mind of the flesh? Do you see how great an opposition of wills his words set before us? For the will of the Spirit is one thing, and the will of the flesh must be understood as another. They are opposed to each other (Galatians 5:17), and they cannot possibly come together into one. When, then, man is of the flesh and the law is spiritual, how could the law even be bearable to those so sick with sin? And this is said very wisely. For if he is of the flesh, he might be thought of as a kind of captive and […]
